title: The exam
points: Three sections of 45 minutes each: Quantitative Reasoning (21 questions, Problem Solving only), Verbal Reasoning (23 questions, Reading Comprehension and Critical Reasoning), Data Insights (20 questions: Data Sufficiency, Table Analysis, Graphics Interpretation, Multi-Source Reasoning, Two-Part Analysis).
You choose the order of the sections before the exam starts, and you may take one optional 10-minute break after the first or second section.
Each section adapts to you question by question: getting questions right leads to harder ones.
You must answer each question to move on; you cannot go back during the section.
You can bookmark questions and, if time is left at the end of a section, review any question and change up to 3 answers.
An on-screen calculator is available only in Data Insights.
Scores: total 205–805, each section 60–90, all three weigh the same.
Unanswered questions at the end of a section lower the score: always answer every question.

title: Pacing
points: Average time per question: Quant about 2:09, Verbal about 1:57, Data Insights about 2:15.
Checkpoints (GMAT Lab’s advice): in Quant, about 7 questions every 15 minutes; in Verbal about 8; in Data Insights about 7.
If a question passes about 3 minutes with no clear path, eliminate what you can, guess, bookmark it and move on.
In the last 2–3 minutes, make sure every remaining question gets an answer.
Reading Comprehension passages take time up front: the first question on a passage takes longer, the next ones less.

title: Bookmarks and answer changes
points: Bookmark only questions where you guessed or were unsure.
At the end, go back to bookmarked questions first.
Change an answer only with a clear reason: first instincts are right more often than second-guessing.
You have at most 3 changes per section, so spend them where you found a concrete error.

title: How to read a Critical Reasoning argument
points: Read the question stem first: it tells you what to look for (weaken, assumption, inference…).
In the argument, find the conclusion, then the premises that support it.
Name the gap: what does the author take for granted?
Predict the answer in your own words before reading the choices.
Eliminate choices that are out of scope, too extreme, or that do the opposite of what is asked.

title: How to read a passage
points: Read for structure: the main point, what each paragraph does, and where the author gives an opinion.
Watch contrast words (however, but, yet, although): the key idea usually follows them.
Keep a short map: one line per paragraph.
Do not memorise details: go back to the text when a question asks for them.
Spend about 2–3 minutes reading a long passage; the questions go faster afterwards.

title: Data Sufficiency in 30 seconds
points: Rephrase the question first.
Statement 1 alone → A or D if sufficient; B, C or E if not.
Statement 2 alone, forgetting statement 1.
Combine only if both are insufficient alone.
Test numbers that the question allows, including 0, negatives and fractions.
